title: Dynamic masking for boundary-aware velocity reconstruction in volumetric particle tracking with moving solids
authors: J. T. Jose, A. Jacobson, D. V. Shenoy, S. H. Frankel, and O. Ram
description: A physics-constrained reconstruction method that accounts for moving solid boundaries when converting volumetric particle tracks into gridded velocity fields.
overview: Moving bodies complicate velocity reconstruction because the physical fluid domain changes in time. LE-DM tracks that moving boundary and reconstructs velocity fields while respecting near-wall kinematics and incompressibility.
method: Volumetric particle tracking, dynamic body masks, one-sided divergence operators, and validation against synthetic and experimental cases.
finding: In the reported near-wall validation, the first-cell reconstruction error decreased from 14.0% to 2.9%.
note: Image cropped from the published paper. Source: Measurement Science and Technology (2026).

title: On the application of refractive index matching to study the buoyancy-driven motion of spheres
authors: J. T. Jose, A. Ben-Harosh, and O. Ram (equal first-author contribution)
description: Experimental characterization of three-dimensional wakes and forces around freely rising spheres using refractive-index-matched tomographic particle tracking.
overview: Rising spheres produce complex three-dimensional wakes that modify both their trajectories and hydrodynamic loading. Refractive-index matching allows optical access to the flow near the moving body.
method: Refractive-index matching, tomographic particle tracking velocimetry, three-dimensional wake visualization, and pressure and load inference.
finding: The experiments examine how increasing sphere diameter changes trajectories and wake organization.
note: Vortex isosurface sequence cropped from the International Journal of Multiphase Flow paper (2026).

title: The dynamics of shock wave propagation far downstream of an abrupt area expansion
authors: Y. Gichon, J. T. Jose, H. Chandravamsi, Y. Evron, and O. Ram (equal first-author contribution)
description: Experiments and numerical analysis reveal how a shock wave develops far downstream of an abrupt duct-area expansion.
overview: Abrupt changes in duct geometry cause transmitted shocks to deform, reflect, and interact with the developing flow. This work investigates how the front recovers downstream.
method: Shock-tube experiments, schlieren imaging, and complementary numerical simulations.
finding: The study develops a predictive description of shock-front evolution downstream of abrupt area expansions.
note: Experimental schlieren frame cropped from Journal of Fluid Mechanics (2024).

title: Effect of expansion geometry on turbulence in axisymmetric pipe flows
authors: J. T. Jose, G. Friedmann, D. Feld, and O. Ram
description: Stereo-PIV measurements compare the turbulence response to abrupt and gradual axisymmetric pipe expansions.
overview: Flow separation and reattachment following changes in cross section govern momentum transport and turbulence production. This work contrasts step and wedge axisymmetric expansions.
method: Refractive-index-matched stereo-PIV and turbulence-statistics analysis in a recirculating flow facility.
finding: The gradual expansion produced broader turbulence production and higher losses than the abrupt step under the conditions studied.
note: Velocity-contour comparison cropped from Physical Review Fluids (2026).

title: Flow, pressure, and aerodynamic loads on an oscillating airfoil undergoing dynamic stall
authors: J. T. Jose, Y. Lu, K. Agarwal, and J. Katz
description: Experiments resolve flow structures, pressure, and aerodynamic loads on an oscillating airfoil during dynamic stall.
overview: Dynamic stall couples unsteady separation and coherent-vortex evolution to rapidly changing aerodynamic forces. The study connects measured flow fields to surface loading.
method: Refractive-index-matched water-tunnel measurements, optical velocimetry, and pressure/force reconstruction.
finding: The analysis connects the convection and eventual detachment of the dynamic-stall vortex to the collapse in lift.
note: Streamline and flow-field panels cropped from AIAA Journal (2026).

title: Interface shape surrounding anisotropic particles held at the liquid–gas interface
authors: A. R. Einhorn, J. T. Jose, A. Zigelman, A. D. Gat, and O. Ram (equal first-author contribution)
description: Measurements and modeling of the liquid–gas interface around particles of anisotropic shape.
overview: Particles at fluid interfaces change the surrounding surface geometry. This study examines how anisotropic particle shape influences the resulting interface deformation.
method: Laboratory-based optical interface measurements and physical modeling.
finding: The work quantifies the connection between particle geometry and fluid-interface shape.
note: An original figure can be added here from the Journal of Fluid Mechanics (2025) paper.

title: Coherent structure transport in turbulent axisymmetric pipe expansions
authors: J. T. Jose, G. Friedmann, and O. Ram
description: Analysis of coherent-structure transport, persistence, and spectral organization in abrupt and gradual pipe expansions.
overview: This companion study focuses on the organization and transport of coherent structures in turbulent axisymmetric expansions.
method: Spectral coherence, vortex-structure diagnostics, and finite-time Lyapunov exponent analysis of experimental velocity measurements.
finding: The study compares how expansion geometry influences coherent-structure transport and persistence.
